projects.title: Blindsight: A Synthetic Visual Cortex for Direct Cortical Stimulation
projects.summary: Inspired by Neuralink's proposed blindsight architecture and conversations with a very close blind friend (hello, Mr. Tredway), this project implements a real-time, biologically grounded model of the primary visual cortex (V1) that transforms live camera input into orientation-selective cortical activity using spiking neurons. The broader aim of the blindsight program is to bypass damaged visual pathways by directly stimulating V1, and this project is meant to demonstrate how something like a camera-based visual input can be encoded into structured, orientation-specific neural activity suitable for targeted cortical stimulation.
projects.description:
This project is a real-time computational model of the primary visual cortex designed to explore how biologically grounded vision systems can process natural video. Built entirely in Python, the system streams live input from a Raspberry Pi camera and converts pixel-level information into spike-based cortical responses using a multi-stage pipeline inspired by known V1 microcircuitry.

Incoming video frames are first preprocessed and passed through orientation-selective Gabor filters arranged in a retinotopic grid. These responses are sparsified and encoded as spike trains using latency coding, where stronger features produce earlier spikes. The encoded spikes are then injected into a synthetic V1 model composed of four orientation columns (0°, 45°, 90°, 135°), each containing four cortical layers (L4, L2/3, L5, L6) populated by thousands of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons connected in a feedforward hierarchy.

Neural activity propagates through the model in discrete time steps, and firing rates from Layer 2/3 are decoded into orientation and strength maps that highlight edges and structure in the original scene. The system achieves near real-time performance at approximately 5 to 7 frames per second, representing a more than 300× speedup over the original MDPI2021 reference model by carefully trading off biological detail for computational efficiency.

The project emphasizes interpretability over learned representations, deliberately avoiding deep convolutional networks in favor of explicit feature extraction, spike timing, and layered cortical dynamics. It serves both as a testbed for spiking neural computation and as a conceptual bridge between classical computer vision, neuroscience, and potential neuroprosthetic applications for visual restoration.
